items.prompt: Two callers load the same pending leave request and both approve it. The second SaveChanges finds the Version changed. What does that caller get?
items.answer: A 409 ProblemDetails telling it to reload the resource and retry
distractors: A 200, and its decision quietly overwrites the first approval
A 412 Precondition Failed, since it sent no If-Match header
A 500 error, because nothing maps DbUpdateConcurrencyException
items.explanation: ConcurrencyExceptionHandler recognises the write conflict and writes a 409 problem body ("Reload it and retry"). Lost updates are what the token prevents, Atlas uses no ETag preconditions, and the global handler is exactly what keeps this from being a 500.

items.prompt: An endpoint modifies a versioned EmploymentContract and calls SaveChangesAsync. Where does its Version number get incremented?
items.answer: In AtlasDbContext, which bumps it for each Modified versioned entry
distractors: In SQLite itself, through a rowversion column it updates on every write
In each endpoint, which must add one before it calls the save
In a database trigger that EnsureCreated adds for versioned tables
items.explanation: Both SaveChanges overrides call BumpVersions, which walks ChangeTracker.Entries<IVersioned>() and increments Version when the state is Modified. SQLite has no rowversion type (the ADR says so), the point of centralising is that no endpoint can forget, and there are no triggers.

items.prompt: Atlas saves a DateTimeOffset of 10:00 at +08:00 and reads it back from SQLite. What does it get?
items.answer: The same instant, 02:00 with a zero offset; the +08:00 is gone
distractors: 10:00 at +08:00, because the offset is stored next to the ticks
10:00 at a zero offset, so the instant moves by eight hours
The same instant, but cut to whole seconds by string parsing
items.explanation: The converter stores value.UtcTicks and reads new DateTimeOffset(ticks, TimeSpan.Zero): same instant, offset discarded. No offset column exists, the UTC ticks keep the instant, and ticks preserve 100 ns precision with no string parsing.

items.prompt: Why does AtlasDbContext convert every DateTimeOffset to a long instead of keeping EF Core's default SQLite mapping?
items.answer: The default is TEXT, which SQLite cannot compare as instants
distractors: SQLite rejects DateTimeOffset columns, so EnsureCreated would fail
Integers take less disk space, which is the main concern of the ADR
The default stores local time, so two servers would disagree on it
items.explanation: ADR 0004: SQLite has no date-time type, EF stores DateTimeOffset as TEXT, and ORDER BY or range filters on those strings get wrong semantics or client evaluation. Table creation works fine with TEXT, size is never mentioned, and the issue is comparison, not local time.

items.prompt: BenefitPlan computes EmployerShare as RoundMoney(MonthlyCost * EmployerContributionRate). How is EmployeeShare computed?
items.answer: MonthlyCost - EmployerShare, so both shares re-add to the cent
distractors: RoundMoney(MonthlyCost * (1 - rate)), rounded on its own
RoundMoney with banker's rounding, to offset the employer's bias
MonthlyCost times the rate, truncated toward zero at two places
items.explanation: BenefitPlan.cs line 42: EmployeeShare => MonthlyCost - EmployerShare. The remainder is never rounded independently, which is why the split always re-adds to the premium. Rounding both sides separately is the drift the ADR forbids, and Atlas uses one AwayFromZero rounding, never banker's rounding or truncation.

items.prompt: What does PayrollCalculator.RoundMoney(2.345m) return?
items.answer: 2.35, because a midpoint is rounded away from zero
distractors: 2.34, because a midpoint is rounded to the even digit
2.345, since RoundMoney keeps three places for FX
2.34, since decimal amounts are truncated, not rounded
items.explanation: RoundMoney is Math.Round(amount, 2, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero), so 2.345 goes to 2.35. Round-to-even (banker's rounding, the .NET default) would give 2.34; the ADR rejects it. RoundMoney always rounds to 2 places, and it rounds rather than truncates.

items.prompt: A client's invoice has several payslip lines in EUR and the client is billed in USD. How does Atlas apply the FX rate?
items.answer: Once, to the summed invoice total, rounding that single product
distractors: Per line, rounding each converted line, then summing the results
At payment time, using the rate on the day the invoice gets paid
Never; invoices are issued only in the payroll country's currency
items.explanation: PayrollAssessment line 66: RoundMoney(total * fxRate). Converting per line and summing rounded lines is the drift the ADR avoids. ADR 0008 uses the period's effective rate at completion, not a payment-day rate, and invoices do carry a TotalInBillingCurrency.

items.prompt: An amendment raising a salary is approved with an EffectiveDate of 15 May. What salary does May's payroll use?
items.answer: The new salary for the whole of May, with no proration by day
distractors: The old salary to 14 May and the new one after, prorated by days
The old salary; a raise starts in the first full month after it
Both, averaged, since two records qualify for the same month
items.explanation: EffectiveForMonth takes the latest record with EffectiveDate on or before the month end, so the 15 May record wins for May. The ADR documents the simplification: a mid-month change owns that whole month. There is no proration, no full-month delay, and no averaging; LastOrDefault picks one record.

items.prompt: A draft May payroll run already exists. An amendment for May is approved afterwards. What do the May payslips show?
items.answer: The snapshot from run creation; the amendment hits the next run
distractors: The new terms, because a draft run recalculates when it completes
The new terms for gross pay and the old ones for the deductions
Nothing yet: the run is locked until an admin recalculates it
items.explanation: ADR 0008: creating the run computes and stores every Payslip, and from that point it is a snapshot; an amendment approved after creation affects the next run. There is no recalculate-draft operation, payslips are not split between old and new terms, and the run is not blocked.

items.prompt: A ClientViewer key asks GET /api/contracts/{id} for a contract owned by a different client. What is the status?
items.answer: 404, exactly as if that contract id did not exist at all
distractors: 403, because the role is too weak to read that other client's data
401, because the key is only valid for its own client
200, with the other client's salary fields masked out
items.explanation: ADR 0003: cross-client access is 404 for reads and writes, and the not-found and not-yours branches are indistinguishable (CanViewClient guards the load). 403 is reserved for a caller who can see the resource but lacks the role; the key is authenticated, so not 401; nothing is returned.

items.prompt: A ClientViewer key tries to approve a leave request that belongs to its own client. What status does it get?
items.answer: 403, since it can see the request but lacks the role to act
distractors: 404, so that a viewer learns nothing at all about that request
409, because the request is not in an approvable state
401, since a viewer key carries no write credentials
items.explanation: ADR 0003: 403 means the caller can see the resource but lacks the role, and viewers attempting any write is the first example. 404 is for other clients' data; 409 is a domain-state conflict, not a role check; the key authenticated fine, so it is not 401.

items.prompt: A ClientAdmin key calls GET /api/contracts?clientId=<another client's id>. What does the code return?
items.answer: 200 and an empty array: both client filters are applied together
distractors: 200 with its own contracts, and the clientId query value ignored
404, as for any other cross-client resource it asks for
403, because the filter names a client it may not see
items.explanation: Lines 27-36 add Where(ClientId == own) and then, when clientId is given, Where(ClientId == clientId); the two ANDed conditions match nothing, so the page is empty. The ADR wording and the comment ("whatever filter they pass") read as if the filter were ignored, but the code does not ignore it. Lists never 403 or 404 by ownership.

items.prompt: A caller asks a paged list endpoint for ?pageSize=500. What happens?
items.answer: A 400 ValidationProblem with an error under the pageSize key
distractors: 200 with 200 rows, the size quietly clamped to the maximum
200 with all 500 rows, since the maximum is only advisory
200 with 50 rows, the default page size used in its place
items.explanation: Pagination.Validate adds errors["pageSize"] when the value is < 1 or > 200 (MaxPageSize) and returns Results.ValidationProblem. The ADR says out-of-range means 400; nothing clamps, nothing ignores the cap, and the default of 50 applies only when pageSize is absent.

items.prompt: Where does a paged Atlas list response put the total count and the page number?
items.answer: In the X-Total-Count, X-Page and X-Page-Size response headers
distractors: In an { items, total } envelope object that wraps the JSON array
In a Link header with rel="next" and rel="last" entries
In a metadata object appended as the last array element
items.explanation: ToPageAsync sets three response headers and returns a plain list, so bodies stay JSON arrays. The ADR rejected the envelope to avoid a breaking change; there is no Link header, and the array holds only items.

items.prompt: An admin deactivates a client's API key. When does that key stop working?
items.answer: On its next request, as every request looks up ApiUsers
distractors: When its issued JWT expires, after the five-minute skew
After an in-memory key cache refreshes, about hourly
Only once the ApiUser row is deleted from the table
items.explanation: HandleAuthenticateAsync queries ApiUsers on every request and fails when !user.IsActive, so revocation is immediate. Atlas issues no JWTs (the ADR lists that as avoided infrastructure), there is no key cache, and keys are revoked by deactivation precisely so rows are never deleted.

items.front: ADR 0005: the rounding rule, worked through payroll and final pay?
items.back: Round once per component, then derive the rest by arithmetic. Payroll: employer cost and deductions are the rounded products; net = gross - deductions and total cost = gross + employer cost, so net + deductions == gross holds exactly. Final pay: the daily rate is rounded once, then multiplied by the days.

items.front: ADR 0003: when does a client admin key get 403, and what guards each load?
items.back: Two 403 cases for a client admin: calling a platform-only endpoint, and writing to a different client's id passed in a request body. Every resource load goes through CanViewClient, and every endpoint applies the same matrix uniformly.

items.front: How Atlas detects a lost update (ADR 0007)?
items.back: IVersioned entities carry a plain int Version, registered as an EF concurrency token for every implementing entity. A stale write, one whose row's Version changed after the entity was loaded, throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException, and a single global ConcurrencyExceptionHandler decides what the caller is told, so no endpoint handles the conflict itself.

items.front: ADR 0008: what creating vs completing a PayrollRun does.
items.back: Create (per country + month, platform admin): computes and stores every Payslip and marks expenses Reimbursed in the same unit of work. Complete (one-way Draft -> Completed): one invoice per client, fee on gross only, FX at the period rate; a missing FX rate fails with 409 and leaves it draft.

items.prompt: Lesson 1's table has contracts A (Acme, PH, Active), B (Acme, US, Active), C (Other company, PH, Active) and D (Acme, PH, Draft). An Acme viewer drops countryCode and sends only status=Active. Which contracts come back?
items.answer: A and B; C matches Active but is outside what Acme may see
distractors: A, B and C; with no country filter, Active alone picks the rows
A only; an omitted country filter falls back to the PH default
A, B and D; dropping one filter also switches off the status one
items.explanation: Lesson 1 (lines 39-41): with the country parameter removed, Acme can receive A and B but still not C, because the ownership rule is always present and optional filters can narrow access but never grant more of it (line 14). C fails ownership whatever filters are sent, D still fails the Active state filter, and nothing substitutes a default country for an omitted one.

items.prompt: The contract-list GET adds the client-ownership Where and then the optional status and country Where calls before paging. What does Lesson 1 say each added Where does?
items.answer: It makes a more specific query that runs only once materialized
distractors: It filters the rows that the previous Where already loaded
It sends one more SQL statement and intersects results in memory
It loads every contract, then drops those outside the caller's client
items.explanation: Lesson 1 line 26: the query is a description until a database operation materializes it, and adding another Where builds a more specific description. It does not query every row and then grant permissions afterward, so no Where loads rows by itself, sends its own statement, or filters an in-memory list.

items.prompt: Country creation trims the name and rejects a 101-character name with a field-specific 400. A reviewer proposes deleting that check because the entity already carries an EF maximum-length annotation. What does Lesson 1 say?
items.answer: Keep the check, as the EF annotation is no substitute for it on SQLite
distractors: Delete it, as the annotation makes SQLite return that same 400 itself
Delete it, as database constraints already give field-specific errors
Keep it, but run it after saving so the constraint gets the first say
items.explanation: Lesson 1 lines 47-52 name two separate responsibilities: API validation gives the user a useful error and refuses values outside the documented contract, while database constraints protect stored relationships and uniqueness even for writers other than this endpoint. An EF maximum-length annotation is not a substitute for the first, especially with SQLite. Validation happens before saving, and the test checks both the 400 and the absence of the rejected row.

items.prompt: You are writing a test that proves worker creation rejects an overlong name. Per Lesson 1, what should the rest of the request body look like?
items.answer: Otherwise valid, so the 400 can only come from the name rule
distractors: Invalid in several fields, so one test covers every rule at once
Empty apart from the name, so no other rule can get in the way
Randomised on each run, so the rule meets many shapes of input
items.explanation: Lesson 1 line 54: the tests use an otherwise valid request at the boundary. If a request has an invalid email, a missing country and an overlong name at the same time, a 400 would not establish which rule worked, so unrelated fields stay valid when proving one rule. Several invalid fields, missing fields or random values each add other possible reasons for the 400.

items.prompt: Currency creation promises three ASCII letters and uppercases accepted text. Why does Lesson 1 insist the ASCII check runs on the original trimmed characters, not the uppercased ones?
items.answer: Uppercasing can map a non-ASCII letter to ASCII and hide the violation
distractors: Uppercasing first would reject lowercase input such as ` usd ` outright
The check must confirm the code is listed in a real currency registry
Checking after uppercasing would let a digit such as the 1 in U1D pass
items.explanation: Lesson 1 line 60: uppercasing first can map a non-ASCII character into an ASCII character in some cases, so normalization would quietly erase the evidence that the original input broke the ASCII-letters-only promise; the tests use a non-ASCII long-s example. Line 58: ` usd ` is accepted and becomes USD, U1D fails shape validation, and a fictional XYZ is accepted because shape, not registry membership, is validated.

items.prompt: The invoice list is filtered with payrollRunId set to a well-formed GUID that matches no payroll run. Per Lesson 1, what does the caller get?
items.answer: An empty matching collection, with the GUID accepted as valid
distractors: A 404, the same as a detail route asked for a missing document
A binding error, as for any GUID text that names no stored row
A database error, raised when the foreign key lookup finds no run
items.explanation: Lesson 1 line 62: the payrollRunId filter accepts a syntactically valid GUID even if no such run exists, and then returns an empty matching collection. A binding error is reserved for malformed GUID text, a 404 is what a detail route returns when one document is missing, and neither case is a database crash.

items.prompt: A contract status filter receives the text `999`, and the enum declares only Draft, Active and Terminated. What does Lesson 1 say Enum.TryParse on its own does with that text?
items.answer: It parses it, which is why the rule adds an Enum.IsDefined check
distractors: It returns false, as 999 matches none of the members declared
It parses it only if the enum carries the [Flags] attribute
It maps 999 to the nearest declared member, here Terminated
items.explanation: Lesson 1 lines 66-68: TryParse answers whether text converts to the enum's underlying representation, and it can successfully parse 999 even when the enum declares only Draft, Active and Terminated. The shared defined-enum rule therefore checks parsing and Enum.IsDefined, and also rejects comma-separated combinations because these filters accept one value, not a flags expression. Nothing maps a number to a nearest member.

items.prompt: The country list takes a nullable Boolean isActive. A first version applies its activity Where only when isActive is true. Which request does that break, per Lesson 1?
items.answer: isActive=false, which then skips the filter and returns every country
distractors: An omitted isActive, which then returns only the active countries
isActive=true, which then also returns the inactive countries
None of them, as a nullable Boolean carries just two meaningful values
items.explanation: Lesson 1 lines 74-82: omitted, true and false are three inputs (do not filter, active countries, inactive countries). A condition that runs only when the value is true loses the false case: false skips the filter and behaves like omitted. The fix checks whether a value was supplied and compares to it, and the currencyCode=USD&isActive=false test proves both filters stay active even when the expected result is empty.

items.prompt: A client prefix search is sent the text `%_`. Per Lesson 1, what should it return, and which test evidence shows it?
items.answer: Names starting with a literal `%_`, shown by a seeded `%_` name
distractors: Every client name, as `%` and `_` act as LIKE wildcards in SQL
A 400, as a prefix may contain only letters, digits and spaces
Accent-folded matches, shown by the happy-path `ac` example
items.explanation: Lesson 1 lines 88-92: the query uses StartsWith rather than concatenating caller text into a LIKE pattern, so a prefix containing `%` or `_` means those literal characters. The tests seed names starting with `%_` and prove the search returns that name rather than every name; a happy-path `ac` example alone would not catch wildcard behavior, and the implementation does not promise accent folding.

items.prompt: A worker list sorts by name and then Id, and several workers share a name. A refactor swaps `.ThenBy(w => w.Id)` for a second `.OrderBy(w => w.Id)`. What changes, per Lesson 1?
items.answer: The Id order replaces the name order instead of breaking its ties
distractors: Nothing changes, as both calls append Id after the existing name order
Tied names become unique, so the paging order is total anyway
The query is refused, as OrderBy may appear once per query
items.explanation: Lesson 1 line 96: a name is not a unique sort key, so the implementation sorts by name, then Id. ThenBy extends an order; a second OrderBy would replace the first order, leaving the list ordered by Id alone. Names are not made unique (line 100 warns against hiding a query-design issue that way), and the lesson describes the second OrderBy as replacing the order, not as an error.

items.prompt: Headcount is requested with a PH filter. A shortcut builds the full report and then removes the non-PH entries from the final country array. What does Lesson 1 say goes wrong?
items.answer: The total and client breakdown still describe every country
distractors: Nothing, provided the PH row equals the database's own count
Only the PH row is wrong, as it was grouped before filtering
The country rows go missing while the totals stay correct
items.explanation: Lesson 1 lines 120-122: the service applies the optional filter before selecting and grouping records, so the total, the country breakdown and the client breakdown all describe the same PH population. Filtering the final country array alone would leave a misleading overall total and client breakdown, which is why the test checks the sum of client counts as well as the visible country rows.

items.prompt: A batch request asks to complete two onboarding checklist items, and the second item belongs to a different contract. Per Lesson 3, what gets saved?
items.answer: Neither item, as every item is checked before any box is ticked
distractors: The first item, as each item is validated and then saved in turn
The first item, with the response listing the second as rejected
Both items, as parent membership is checked once the save is done
items.explanation: Lesson 3 lines 9-16: the batch endpoint first checks the entire request (permission, item count, duplicate IDs, note lengths, parent membership, versions and completion state) and only then changes the validated items and saves them together. A loop that validates and saves one item at a time could leave the first item complete when the second fails, which the two-phase design exists to prevent; nothing is partly applied.

items.prompt: The batch endpoint compares each item's expected version early, and EF's UPDATE also puts the original Version in its WHERE clause. Why does Lesson 3 keep both checks?
items.answer: One catches staleness at load time, the other changes made after it
distractors: The early check suffices, and the WHERE clause only feeds logging
The WHERE clause suffices, and the early check only speeds up tests
Both repeat one test, kept twice in case one is deleted by mistake
items.explanation: Lesson 3 line 53: the early expected-version check gives a clear failure when a request is already stale at load time, and the database condition (UPDATE ... WHERE Version = original, lines 41-49) catches changes that happen after that check. You need both because they operate at different moments; neither one alone covers both windows, and neither is a duplicate kept for safety.

items.prompt: An admin renames a country's onboarding template item from "Identity check" to "Photo ID and identity check". Per Lesson 3, what happens to a contract created in that country yesterday?
items.answer: It keeps yesterday's title, and only later contracts get the new one
distractors: Its checklist row is renamed, as rows point at the template item
Its row is renamed once the template header's version is bumped
Its row is dropped and rebuilt from the template on the next read
items.explanation: Lesson 3 lines 71-75: a new contract copies template values into its own checklist rows, and `new OnboardingItem` allocates new IDs and independent state. The template is configuration and the rows are copied work, so a contract created yesterday keeps yesterday's title and one created tomorrow receives the new title. Rows do not reuse template item IDs, and neither a version bump nor a read re-applies the template.

items.prompt: A contract-creation request reads "country active" while another request pauses hiring in that country. How does Lesson 3 stop the creation from saving on its stale observation?
items.answer: Creation also touches Country.Version, so the stale writer conflicts
distractors: Creation re-reads the country inside a lock that the pause holds
The pause cancels in-flight creations by deleting their drafts
The contract's own Version detects the pause at the moment the save runs
items.explanation: Lesson 3 lines 83-87: creation and activation touch Country.Version when saving and the pause changes the same country row, so a writer using a stale country version conflicts; Country is the common record on which the competing decisions meet. The stated tradeoff is that unrelated hiring operations in one country may conflict and need a reload. No lock or cancellation is involved, and a contract's own Version is not the row the pause changes.

items.prompt: Two new leave requests both read "five days remaining", each reserve four days and insert separate rows. Per learning note 08, why does Atlas's version token not catch this?
items.answer: Neither insert updates a shared existing row whose version could clash
distractors: The token is checked on approval only, and both requests are pending
SQLite serializes the inserts, so the second sees the lower balance
It does catch it, and the second insert gets a 409 like any stale write
items.explanation: Learning note 08 line 11: two new leave requests can both read five days remaining, reserve four days each and insert different rows, and their own version tokens cannot conflict because they update no shared existing row. A stronger guarantee may need a shared balance/version row, suitable isolation or another database-backed coordination policy. The version check catches decisions made on stale loaded state (line 9); it does not serialize inserts or turn this into a 409.

items.front: ADR 0001: what does SQLite with EnsureCreated (no migrations) buy Atlas, and what does it give up?
items.back: Gains: zero setup (dotnet run/test need no installed services; resetting dev data is deleting atlas.db; each test fixture holds its own in-memory connection open) and tests that run real SQL (unique indexes, FKs, concurrency tokens) instead of the EF in-memory provider's approximations. Cost: no migration history, so a schema change means recreating the database; a production deployment would move to migrations and likely PostgreSQL.

items.front: ADR 0011: what do /health, /health/live and /health/ready each check, and why add a live probe?
items.back: /health is preserved and still includes database connectivity; /health/live has no dependency checks; /health/ready runs the checks tagged ready, today database connectivity only. All three are anonymous. Reason: a restart probe on a database-checking endpoint could restart a perfectly responsive process during a dependency outage.

items.front: ADR 0011: how does Atlas connect a caller's error to a log line, and what is that mechanism not?
items.back: The server request id is sent as the X-Request-Id header, carried in ProblemDetails as traceId, and written in the completion log; request logging sits outside error handling so the log records the final status of handled failures. It is request correlation, not end-to-end distributed tracing, and secrets and payloads stay out of the request logs.

items.front: ADR 0010: how are report responsibilities split between ReportEndpoints and ReportService?
items.back: ReportEndpoints keeps authorization and binding and validates query inputs before any arithmetic; optional dates are resolved with TimeProvider and passed, with cancellation, as explicit values into an API-local ReportService, which uses read-only projections for payroll costs and invoice aging. DTO names and JSON shapes stay the same, and no interface is added just to mirror the one implementation.

items.front: Learning note 04: what do Select, Include, tracking and AsNoTracking each contribute to a report query?
items.back: Select projects only the columns needed (a navigation value such as a run's year and month can be projected without loading the full entity); Include loads related entities; tracking lets EF detect changes for SaveChanges, which a report does not need. A scalar projection already avoids tracking, and an explicit AsNoTracking also communicates the read-only intent.

items.front: Learning note 04: what evidence backs a claim that an index makes a query faster, and what does the index cost?
items.back: Inspect the SQL (EF logging or ToQueryString), noting filters, joins, selected columns, ordering and rows returned; compare the query plan before and after on representative data and report the dataset size. An index helps particular lookups but adds storage and write work, and its existence alone does not prove a query uses it.

items.front: Lesson 1: what does BootcampApiFactory's fixed clock replace in the birth-date tests, and what stays real?
items.back: It supplies a fixed 1 September 2026 so the tests prove 1 September is allowed and 2 September rejected on any day they run. It replaces only the external time dependency: the production handler still runs the real date comparison, and the tests still call the HTTP endpoint and inspect persistence. Avoid computing "tomorrow" once from the real clock.

items.front: Lesson 3: where do a contract note's author and timestamp come from, and does adding a note change Contract.Version?
items.back: The author is the authenticated principal and the timestamp comes from the clock; the body carries only the note text, so a body naming another author is ignored. Appending a note leaves Contract.Version unchanged: a general note alters neither employment terms nor the contract lifecycle. Notes are visible to client viewers and have no API edit or delete routes.
